ACTION: ADD 1
TITLE: Evaluating Current Detectors on RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Re-evaluate existing membership inference methods (e.g., Perplexity, Min-K% Prob) on real-world LLM benchmarks with RL-phase contamination introduced via additional training with randomly sampled RLVR rewards for a subset of test cases. Compare the detection accuracy of these methods in the RL-phase contamination case to their reported accuracy in pre-trained and SFT stages.
CONTROLS: 
- Run each detector in the relevant pre-training and SFT stage to serve as a control.
- Include a baseline of a blind detector that always predicts contamination.
- Measure the effect of sample size on detector accuracy, by repeating the evaluation with smaller training sets.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Current detectors will generally fail to detect RL-phase contamination, as their likelihood-based signals are weakened; however, some detectors may perform surprisingly well on certain benchmarks due to coincidence in detection signals.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Investigating Token-Level Entropy Patterns in RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Examine the distribution of token-level entropy in a set of LLMs trained with RL phase, comparing contaminants (that were part of the RL training data) to non-contaminants (never seen during RL training). Investigate whether specific pattern anomalies (e.g. entropy concentration on certain tokens, early entropy collapse) can reliably distinguish contaminants from non-contaminants.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to baseline models without RL phase, to confirm that the patterns are specific to RL training dynamics.
- Include a control to evaluate the impact of RL phase duration and reward sparsity on token-level entropy patterns.
- Apply and evaluate entropy-based detectors on this dataset, to assess whether these patterns can be leveraged for contamination detection.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: While token-level entropy patterns may exhibit anomalies for contaminants, they may not be reliable or generalizable across all models and tasks, due to variability in the patterns and the LLM's internal state.

ACTION: ADD 3
TITLE: Modeling Policy Collapse in RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Propose a probabilistic framework for modeling policy collapse in RL-trained LLMs, and evaluate whether the framework can be used to distinguish between contaminants and non-contaminants. Specifically, develop a generative model that captures the distribution of policy collapse patterns in the context of RL training, and test its ability to detect contamination by generating and comparing embeddings or representations of contaminants and non-contaminants.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to a baseline model that ignores policy collapse, to evaluate the effectiveness of the framework in detecting contamination.
- Include a control to evaluate the impact of RL phase duration and reward sparsity on policy collapse patterns.
- Apply and evaluate the policy collapse framework as a detector on the token-level entropy patterns dataset from proposal 2.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (including training the generative model)
PREDICTION: The framework may show promising results in detecting contamination via policy collapse, but may require fine-tuning to accommodate specific reward structures and LLM architectures.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Investigating Token-Level Entropy Patterns in RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal by incorporating a clustering analysis to identify distinct token-level entropy patterns that are specifically associated with RL phase contamination. Employ dimensionality reduction techniques (e.g., PCA, t-SNE) to visualize and explore the underlying structure of the entropy patterns. Investigate whether specific clusters can be used to develop unbiased estimators of contamination likelihood.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to baseline models without RL phase, to confirm that the patterns are specific to RL training dynamics.
- Include a control to evaluate the impact of RL phase duration and reward sparsity on token-level entropy patterns.
- Evaluate the performance of the clustering-based estimator on a separate test set.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (same as before, with just additional analysis steps)
PREDICTION: The refined analysis may enable a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between token-level entropy patterns and RL phase contamination, potentially leading to the development of effective and generalizable detectors.

ACTION: ADD 4
TITLE: Synthetic Benchmarking for RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Develop a set of synthetic LLM benchmarks specifically designed to simulate RL phase contamination, allowing for controlled evaluation of contamination detection methods in a data-efficient manner. Create a range of scenarios with varying degrees of contamination (e.g., small, large, and mixed) and reward structures (e.g., sparse, dense). Use these benchmarks to systematically evaluate the performance of existing and proposed contamination detection methods, such as those developed in previous proposals.
CONTROLS: 
- Include baselines using deterministic and probabilistic contamination simulation methods.
- Evaluate the transferability of detectors across different synthetic scenarios.
- Compare the performance of detectors on synthetic benchmarks to their performance on real-world data from proposal 1.
COST: 150 GPU-hours (sequential estimating synthetic scenarios)
PREDICTION: Synthetic benchmarking may provide a valuable tool for assessing the reliability and generalizability of contamination detection methods, helping to identify areas for improvement and optimizing detector development for real-world applications.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Evaluating Current Detectors on RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Refine the proposal by incorporating an ablation study to investigate the effectiveness of different detector components (e.g., pre-training, SFT, RL phase) in capturing contamination signals. Specifically, experiment with removing or modifying each component to assess its contribution to detector accuracy. This will help identify the key factors driving contamination detection in the current detectors and inform the development of more effective methods for RL phase contamination.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to the original baseline results for current detectors.
- Include controls to evaluate the impact of sample size and data quality on detector performance.
- Assess the sensitivity of detector accuracy to specific detector parameters (e.g., kernel type, hyperparameters).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (no additional training, just re-running existing experiments)
PREDICTION: The ablation study may provide valuable insights into the strengths and weaknesses of current detectors, highlighting potential areas for improvement and enabling the development of more effective and robust contamination detection methods.

ACTION: ADD 5
TITLE: Transfer-Learning Inspired Detectors for RL Phase Contamination
PROPOSAL: Explore the use of transfer-learning based approaches to detect RL phase contamination, building upon the insights from the synthetic benchmarking (proposal 4) and the ablation study (revised proposal 1). Investigate whether pre-trained models and fine-tuning strategies can be leveraged to adapt existing detectors to the RL phase contamination domain, or whether new, specifically designed models are required for effective detection.
CONTROLS: 
- Compare to the performance of the original detectors evaluated in proposal 1.
- Include controls to evaluate the impact of pre-training on detector accuracy and robustness.
- Assess the transferability of detectors across different synthetic scenarios.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (including fine-tuning existing models)
PREDICTION: Transfer-learning may provide a promising approach for detecting RL phase contamination, leveraging the strengths of existing models and facilitating the development of robust and generalizable detectors.

ACTION: ADD 6
TITLE: Adversarial Attacks for Evaluating Contamination Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop and apply adversarial attacks to test the robustness of contamination detection methods, specifically targeting the RL phase contamination scenarios studied in the synthetic benchmarking (proposal 4) and the transfer-learning inspired detectors (proposal 5). Investigate whether the proposed detectors can resist or are vulnerable to various types of attacks, and explore the development of defense strategies to enhance their robustness.
CONTROLS: 
- Include baselines using state-of-the-art adversarial attack methods for membership inference.
- Evaluate the impact of different attack strengths and strategies on detector performance.
- Assess the transferability of detector robustness across different synthetic scenarios.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (including training and testing attack methods)
PREDICTION: The adversarial attack evaluations may provide valuable insights into the resilience of contamination detection methods against stealthy threats, enabling the development of more robust and reliable detectors that can withstand real-world adversarial attacks.

- Assess the transferability of detector accuracy across different augmented datasets.
- Use the augmented datasets to re-evaluate and refine existing contamination detection methods.

PROPOSAL: Investigate the reinforcement learning post-training dynamics to identify distinctive patterns or behaviors that distinguish training and unseen problems.

ACTION: ADD 2
TITLE: Reward-Based Traffic Shift Detection
PROPOSAL: Develop a detectorspecifically designed for reward-driven training phases using reward-based traffic shift analysis, which observes if the distribution of the model's outputs has shifted significantly after RL training.
CONTROLS: Compare the output distributions of the same model before and after RL training by computing metrics like Jensen-Shannon divergence or Kullback-Leibler divergence between the pre- and post-RL training output distributions on a holdout set.
COST: 50 GPU-hours for calculating metrics and comparing output distributions (per dataset and model combination).
PREDICTION: Detect a significant distribution shift for most test cases but may fail to detect contamination in cases where the reward function provides strong guidance to the model, ironing out the original training dataset's impact.

CONTROLS: In addition to computing metrics like Jensen-Shannon divergence, compare the overlap of the pre-training and RL training data samples embedded in the model's output distribution.
COST: 100 GPU-hours for calculating metrics and comparing output distributions with overlap measurements (per dataset and model combination).
PREDICTION: With the revised approach, expected to detect contamination in cases where a model has seen pre-training data and to improve the overall detection rate for a broader range of test cases. However, may still struggle with very difficult test cases where contamination is subtle and effectively masked by the strong rewards.

PROPOSAL: Implement out-of-distribution (OOD) detection techniques to improve contamination detection methods and make them more robust against variable environmental conditions and outliers.

title: theoretical framework for rl contamination detection using reward signal analysis

We show that contamination can be identified by analyzing the distance between these encoded reward signals. We also provide an efficient algorithm for computing these embedding functions, and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on simulated data.
CONTROLS: comparison with existing contamination detection methods, experimental validation using synthetic data
